lessons.title: The European Cup begins
lessons.subtitle: An invitational tournament becomes a continental stage

story.title: A new European contest
story.body: The competition now known as the UEFA Champions League began in the 1955/56 season. Its original name was the European Champion Clubs’ Cup, a direct description of its aim: bring leading club sides from different countries into one European contest.

story.title: A small field, a lasting idea
story.body: That first edition was an invitational tournament with 16 teams. Clubs were invited to take part, so the opening field was not yet the modern qualifying path from national leagues. The competition’s name and entry system would change, but the idea of a European club champion started here.

facts.label: Inaugural field size

lessons.title: From groups to one league phase
lessons.subtitle: The Champions League changes shape

story.title: A new name and a new stage
story.body: The European Cup introduced its first group stage in 1991/92. The Champions League name followed in 1992/93. These are separate milestones: a change in the tournament structure, followed by the identity associated with its next era.

story.title: A shared table
story.body: Beginning in 2024/25, the group stage gave way to a league phase with 36 clubs. Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents: four at home and four away. Unlike a traditional round-robin league, clubs do not face every other participant.

facts.label: Champions League era
facts.scope: Champions League branding; 1992/93
facts.evidence: Official UEFA excerpt: “Champions League from the 1992/93 season”

facts.label: Different opponents
facts.scope: UEFA Champions League; format introduced in 2024/25
facts.evidence: Official UEFA excerpt: “eight matches against eight different teams”

story.title: A steep half-time deficit
story.body: At half-time of the 2005 final in Istanbul, AC Milan led Liverpool 3–0. Liverpool answered with three goals in seven minutes, leveling the match at 3–3 and carrying it into extra time.

story.title: A champion decided by penalties
story.body: Neither team scored in extra time, so the final went to a penalty shoot-out. Liverpool won the shoot-out 3–2 and lifted the trophy after one of the competition’s most memorable comebacks. Keep the match score separate from the shoot-out score: 3–3, then Liverpool 3–2 on penalties.

facts.label: Half-time score

facts.label: Penalty shoot-out score

facts.evidence: Official UEFA excerpt: “Liverpool win 3-2 on penalties”

story.title: A single top division
story.body: On July 28, 1962, the German Football Association voted to introduce a national single-division top flight. The plan brought a new national competition together from the regional structure that had preceded it.

story.title: The first season
story.body: The Bundesliga began in 1963/64 with 16 clubs. That inaugural season established the league as Germany’s national top division. The start date, its nationwide structure, and its opening field size explain what made the new competition different.

facts.label: Founding decision
facts.scope: DFB decision to establish the Bundesliga; 28 July 1962
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “28 July 1962”

facts.label: First season
facts.scope: Inaugural Bundesliga season
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “first season began in August 1963”

facts.prompt: How many clubs played in the first Bundesliga season?
facts.label: Inaugural clubs
facts.scope: Bundesliga; inaugural season 1963/64
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “16 teams”

story.title: The first expansion
story.body: The Bundesliga expanded from 16 to 18 clubs in 1965/66. The 18-club setup became the familiar shape of the competition, though one historic season would briefly make the league larger.

story.title: One season of 20 clubs
story.body: After German reunification, the 1991/92 Bundesliga admitted 20 clubs, including the East German sides Hansa Rostock and Dynamo Dresden. The league returned to 18 teams the following season, 1992/93. That temporary change tied league size to a major national turning point.

facts.label: Return to 18 teams

lessons.title: Leverkusen’s unbeaten season
lessons.subtitle: The 2023/24 champions finish without a loss

story.title: A first for the league
story.body: Bayer Leverkusen clinched their first Bundesliga title on Matchday 29 of the 2023/24 season. They kept winning and drawing after securing the championship, then completed all 34 league matches without a defeat.

story.title: An unbeaten campaign
story.body: Leverkusen finished the 2023/24 Bundesliga with 28 wins, six draws, and zero losses. It was the first time a team completed a full Bundesliga season unbeaten. The feat belongs to that completed season, not to an ongoing record that could change.

facts.prompt: On which matchday did Leverkusen clinch the 2023/24 Bundesliga title?
facts.label: Title-clinching matchday
facts.scope: Bayer Leverkusen; Bundesliga 2023/24
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “on Matchday 29 out of 34”

facts.prompt: How many Bundesliga matches did Leverkusen win in their 2023/24 unbeaten season?
facts.label: League wins
facts.scope: Bayer Leverkusen; Bundesliga 2023/24, 34 matches
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “28 wins, six draws and zero defeats”

facts.prompt: How many defeats did Leverkusen record in their 2023/24 Bundesliga season?
facts.label: League defeats
facts.scope: Bayer Leverkusen; Bundesliga 2023/24, 34 matches
facts.evidence: Official Bundesliga excerpt: “first team to complete an entire Bundesliga season without defeat”

lessons.title: The roots of Mexico’s top flight
lessons.subtitle: A professional league, then a new identity

story.title: The professional roots
story.body: Mexico’s professional First Division began in 1943/44. This is the historical starting point of the top flight. Its Spanish name, Primera División, describes its place at the top of the domestic league structure.

story.title: The Liga MX identity
story.body: The Liga MX project was presented in 2012. That modern identity came decades after the first professional season. Keep the two dates separate: 1943/44 for the professional roots, and 2012 for the Liga MX launch.

facts.prompt: What was the first season of Mexico’s professional First Division?
facts.label: First professional season
facts.scope: Mexican professional First Division; inaugural season
facts.evidence: Chivas official history dates the professional First Division’s beginning to 1943-44.

facts.prompt: What Spanish name describes the historical Mexican First Division?
facts.label: Historical competition name
facts.scope: Mexican professional top flight; historical identity
facts.evidence: Chivas official history identifies the professional First Division, translated as Primera División.

facts.prompt: In which year was the Liga MX project presented?
facts.label: Liga MX identity
facts.scope: Liga MX project presentation; June 2012
facts.evidence: El Informador’s on-site report, dated June 5, 2012, documents Decio de María’s presentation of Liga MX.

lessons.title: Two title races
lessons.subtitle: From Invierno and Verano to Apertura and Clausura

story.title: A split calendar
story.body: Mexico’s short-tournament era began with Invierno 1996. The structure created two title races within a football season. The first labels were Invierno and Verano: winter and summer.

story.title: Read the tournament label
story.body: Later editions use Apertura and Clausura. A championship belongs to its named tournament, so a year alone is not enough to identify the title. Some editions have special names, including Bicentenario and Guard1anes. Read the full label before comparing winners.

facts.prompt: How many title races did the short-tournament structure create within a football season?
facts.label: Title races per season
facts.scope: Mexican short-tournament structure introduced in 1996; individual editions can be cancelled
facts.evidence: Claro Sports describes the 1996 format as allowing two champions in a football season.

facts.prompt: What were the short tournaments first called?
facts.label: Original tournament names
facts.scope: Mexican First Division; initial short-tournament names from 1996
facts.evidence: Claro Sports lists the early editions as Invierno and Verano.

facts.prompt: Which pair of names is used for later opening and closing tournaments?
facts.label: Later tournament names
facts.scope: Liga MX tournament labels; some editions have special names
facts.evidence: Claro Sports documents later editions as Apertura and Clausura, alongside special tournament names.

lessons.title: Santos and the short-tournament era
lessons.subtitle: A first crown and the people behind it

story.title: A new era’s first winner
story.body: Santos Laguna won Invierno 1996, the first title in the short-tournament era and the club’s first league championship. Jared Borgetti arrived for that tournament and scored 16 goals in the title-winning campaign.

story.title: A champion returns as coach
story.body: Benjamín Galindo was a player in that first Santos championship. He later returned as the coach who won Clausura 2012. The two milestones connect a person to one club across different roles and generations.

facts.prompt: Which club won the first short-tournament title in 1996?
facts.label: Invierno 1996 champion
facts.scope: Mexican First Division; Invierno 1996
facts.evidence: Claro Sports identifies Santos Laguna as the inaugural short-tournament champion.

facts.label: Borgetti’s goals
facts.scope: Jared Borgetti; Santos Laguna; Invierno 1996
facts.evidence: Santos’s official biography records Borgetti’s 16 goals in the club’s first title-winning tournament.

facts.prompt: After winning as a player in Invierno 1996, which Santos title did Benjamín Galindo win as coach?
facts.label: Galindo’s coaching title
facts.scope: Benjamín Galindo; Santos Laguna; coaching championship
facts.evidence: Santos’s official biography distinguishes Galindo’s player title in Invierno 1996 from his coaching title in Clausura 2012.
